title: Flock's CEO Faced Me After Its Cameras Led to My Wrongful Stop
description: Flock CEO Garrett Langley sat down to discuss the errors that led to police stopping me and the growing fight over Flock's network of AI-powered surveillance cameras.
fullText:
Millions of people have seen the story of Flock cameras tracking me in a $155,000 Range Rover and subsequently four police officers surrounding my wife and me in a parking lot. Human error was involved, but Flock cameras working off the company’s AI tech compounded everything at an exponential rate.

Now on the latest episode of The Drivecast, Flock Safety Founder and CEO Garrett Langley sat down with me for a candid discussion about what happened to me and countless others in the last few years, the future vision for Flock amid the public backlash over privacy and Fourth Amendment concerns, the growing calls for regulation, and his previous comment that people who destroy or vandalize Flock equipment are “domestic terrorists.”

On a daily basis there’s reporting of cops misusing Flock’s tech to stalk people, which in turn ends up getting them arrested and sent to jail, misread situations taking place, arguments at city council meetings, and people targeting the automatic license plate readers and cutting them down, shooting them, covering them with trash bags and more. You might call this a hot topic, and somehow, I landed right in the middle of it.

New here? The Drivecast is The Drive‘s weekly podcast that takes you behind-the-scenes on the largest controversies, stories, and characters shaping the automotive industry along with the way our roads look today. Powered by The Drive‘s inside access, original reporting, exclusives, and insights, The Drivecast aims to make everyone an insider.

Listen to The Drivecast via Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or Amazon Music. Love it? Like it? Want to help? Leave a five-star review on your platform of choice to help get The Drivecast in front of more people. Have a suggestion, tip, request, or feedback? Drop us a line at feedback@thedrive.com. I promise, we read every single email.

Joel: Garrett, thank you for agreeing to come on the podcast. I know you’re extremely busy and there’s a lot of controversy at the moment surrounding Flock. You’re living your life on an airplane, even though you’re a family man. Just to get it out of the way and start, aside from a thank you, typically every executive we’ve had on this podcast, I kind of know them. I’ve worked in the industry for 15 years, so I usually know them, we’ve had a relationship. This is the first time I’ve ever met you. Given the podcast and everything, I have to ask: Are you a car enthusiast? Do you like cars? Do you care about driving? I’m genuinely curious.

Garrett: I hate to spoil it for your fans. I am not a car guy. Now, I have a deep appreciation for F1, and that’s more from an athletic standpoint. You look at the sheer engineering behind it—they’re optimizing every single millisecond, every single millimeter of the engine and of the design. But funny enough, up until two or three years ago, I was driving the same Toyota Prius that I’ve been driving since college. Everyone was like, “Why don’t you drive another car?” It works. It works really well. Gets me from A to B. It’s a great car. I wound up upgrading the dash to have Apple CarPlay, because the Toyota didn’t have it, so I retrofit that myself. But no, I get a hard time from some of my friends who love cars, saying that I should be more into cars. Between three kids, a wife, and a business, I’m trying to find time for the simpler things in life.

Joel: I can appreciate that. I didn’t really know what you were going to answer, because the reality is that you’re not a car company, you’re not a supplier of car parts or any of that stuff, so I think it was just context. By the way, a Prius, a Corolla, a Camry—there’s nothing really wrong with them. They’re not enthusiast cars, but to your point, if you’re looking for fuel-efficient, safe, reliable, get you from point A to point B, it’s hard to beat, specifically a Prius. The most recent one looks awesome.

Obviously, I have 99 million questions. There is zero chance we could ever cover all the topics today in the short period of time that you and I have together. I have to start with my situation, because that’s how we got here. There’s no way we could not discuss this. I don’t want to sit and belabor anything. You’ve read the stories, I’m sure you’re up to speed on what happened. I’ve written the stories, I’m well-versed with what happened. I’ve spent countless hours on the phone with your Chief Communications Officer, Josh—super nice guy.

As a recap, if you’re one of the millions of people that did not read the story or hear the podcast, a human error led to a police officer entering incorrectly an incomplete plate number into the National Crime Information Center database. That is managed by the FBI; that’s what all the police from across the nation pull from. That is also what gets fed into automatic license plate readers. Whether it’s Flock, Leonardo, or Axon, Garrett’s team doesn’t have its own database; they’re pulling from the FBI Criminal National Information Center database.

They were fed bad, partial, incorrect information. The system was told, “Go look for a license plate of 34DTM.” It was told to do that. It found it, but the problem was that the one it found—the one on my press car that week, a $155,000 Range Rover—also had a ’10’ in there. Flock saw it, the system saw it. It wasn’t asked about a ’10’, it wasn’t programmed to care about a ’10’, it was programmed to find the bone that it was asked to find. It did, and basically it fed it to the police. The local police then didn’t do the back-end loop, and they did not cross-check the actual plate. There was a photo of the plate, I saw it, they showed it to me, it had ’10’ on it. They either didn’t know what to do with it, they disregarded it, they didn’t enter it into the system. They looked at my plate, they didn’t understand the ’10’, and then they looked at my plate and thought I performed Grand Theft Auto, which I did not.

Basically, we had human error that led into Flock as a technology exponentially increasing the rate at which that error spread, but it wasn’t the source of the error. Then human error on the back end of that loop, not cross-referencing it. A compounding amount of issues at hand.

You can’t change human error; that’s not your job. What I am curious about is, I know Josh mentioned you guys talked to the FBI who manages NCIC, and he tried to talk to the LA police that entered the incorrect information. I’m curious from this situation: What will Flock as a company take away, what have they learned, and what changes will we learn from my edge case? We learn from edge cases.

Garrett: One, I appreciate you sharing and hitting on the facts, which is that there were a lot of things that went wrong. It’s easy to potentially try to aggregate that down to “Flock did this,” and a lot of mistakes happened to create this edge case. Sadly, you weren’t the first person who’s had an edge case, and to your point, Joel, the biggest issue remains this national database at the FBI called NCIC, and how archaic its structure is. There’s no feedback loop mechanisms; it’s really just a static comma-separated file.

We’ve tried to build around it. We have this concept called “suppression.” A local agency—let’s take Atlanta, where I live—might see that there’s a stolen plate out of California, but it’s already been resolved because it’s a rental car or a dealer car. They can, in Flock, suppress that: “Never alert us on that for the next year.” That’s to get around the fact that they can’t force another agency to remove it from NCIC.

Ideally, the way it would work is if enough agencies—let’s call it one, two, or three—flag a tag as no longer valid or a bad entry, it should just get removed. Or at least it should get pushed more aggressively by the FBI. For us, we maintain a productive relationship with the FBI. They obviously play a critical role in broader public safety, and I’m hopeful that they’ll see there’s an opportunity to make something like NCIC, which is an important tool not just for companies like Flock, but for police departments to work together, start to make some enhancements to modernize what’s a central part of our policing system.

Joel: I’m curious because you said something I hadn’t heard yet, whether talking to the chief of police or Josh. When my situation occurred, one of the things I learned from my local police that this all went down with is they asked me where I was going to drive the car, if I was going to drive to other suburbs. I said yes. They warned me that other police officers might be trained differently—Minneapolis might be more aggressive, they might show up with guns drawn, which mine didn’t.

They warned me that I have the case number and my police officer’s name that went through everything with me, and they’re like, “In Plymouth, you have a safety net now; you’re not going to get flagged. But if you go into another suburb with Flock, it’s going to flag you again because it’s pulling from the NCIC.” If Plymouth had done the suppression thing you just mentioned, that doesn’t translate to the Minneapolis Police Department.

Garrett: No, it only impacts Plymouth, because we don’t necessarily want to make a decision on behalf of Minneapolis or Los Angeles. We very much have this structural viewpoint that local decisions should stay local. Plymouth made a decision to suppress that, that’s their right to do that, but that doesn’t impact Minneapolis’s setup.

Joel: Do you believe that in this situation, Plymouth police quickly realized—”quickly” is a relative term in the scheme of life—in the scheme of that day, my wife will tell you so, but do you think that, to your point about the NCIC database, Plymouth police told me the only ones in the situation that could have updated that partial plate in the system would be the officer’s unit? In this case, it was the LA Sheriff’s Department, Malibu Lost Hills station. They’re the only ones that can update that issue. Do you think that as you are talking with NCIC and the FBI about how to modernize the system, it should be able to allow Plymouth police, if they run this down and talk to LA and figure out the situation, to correct this? We shouldn’t have to have this weird loop of Jaguar having to call LA.

Garrett: A proposed solution would be one where—let’s make it you and me so it’s easier and fewer words. Garrett puts in a tag “FEDER” as a stolen car. If Joel says, “Wait a second, I just pulled that person over, that’s not valid anymore,” you should have the ability to say, “I think this should be removed.”

Then to me, I should have some clock—called a day, a week—to say, “No, Joel, you are wrong, I want to keep this.” That to me makes a lot more sense, where you have the ability to say, “Hey, I should delete this,” and I go, “Okay, well I can either let it disappear because I’m not going to fight it, or I could choose to say there’s a reason why that you might have misunderstood.”

I agree with you, there needs to be more collaboration. That’s how more modern systems work. Similarly on our side, I think to your point…

Joel: To be clear, in this situation where I’m Feder and you’re Garrett with the license, are you talking about you as Flock, or you as the FBI NCIC?

Garrett: Us as police departments. Let’s make it easier: I’m LA County, I enter in FEDER as this stolen car. You’re Plymouth and you’re like, “I don’t think it’s stolen anymore, this looks normal.” You should be able to say, “I think it needs to be deleted.” As LA County, I should have a day or a week to say, “No, it is really stolen,” or it automatically gets deleted and removed from the list.

Inevitably what happens is, let’s take the rental car example: A car is reported stolen by the rental car agency. I’m LA County and I put it in NCIC. But then, low and behold, the car was returned a month later. It was not stolen, someone just forgot to return it or something. To me, there’s either an expiration—if you look at the way the Flock system works, which is a little bit different than NCIC, we require an expiration period. You can’t just put something into a list forever. It either is going to be there for 7 days, 30 days, 90 days—you have to define this expiration. I think that would also be a meaningful and positive change to NCIC, to have a 7-day or 30-day max expiration period so that you don’t wind up with this stale data in the system like you experienced.

Joel: Last question on this topic. Flock has an expiration, but NCIC doesn’t. So in this case, let’s make believe in some timeline that didn’t happen and my wife got a manicure that day. She would have been much happier. If 34DTM had been in the system and not gotten pulled over, you’re pulling from NCIC, it wasn’t in the Flock database. You said there are expirations, it can’t be searching forever. How does that work if it’s not expiring out of the NCIC?

Garrett: Here’s a good example: Let’s take Plymouth. Let’s say Plymouth has reasonable suspicion that Feder’s license plate was associated with a residential burglary. They could create on their local version a hot list entry to say, “Hey, this is our Plymouth-only hot list.” There’s NCIC, and we force an expiration on the local level. I think it would be great if NCIC had a similar expiration requirement of, let’s call it a week or a month, so that as a criminal investigator, every month you have to reconfirm, “Yes, I am still looking for this car, it is still an active investigation.” I think that would help a lot. It puts more onus on law enforcement, but your story is a prime one of why the extra work by the law enforcement agency is worth it. It’s not that much work relative to your experience.

Joel: Got it. Let’s pivot from my experience into the future of here and now, and where we go from here, but staying on my topic a little as a joiner setup.

Josh made mention—and it’s all over your website—that there’s a 99% success rate. I don’t want to sit here and question that, so let’s use that in this scenario. You guys are doing about—these are round numbers to be clear, because they’re big—20 billion reads a month. 20 billion reads a month and a 99% success rate means there’s a 1% error rate, misread rate, call it whatever you want to call it. 1% of 20 billion, which is a huge number, is a huge number. I was one of them. Now, I wasn’t a misread, to be clear, but it was an error situation with a bad outcome that ended up with an outcome we don’t want.

What exactly are we doing, what’s Flock doing, what’s being done to bring down that 1% error rate so we’re not at 200 million? Which sounds like an immense number—not an immense number when you have 20 billion, but it’s still a big number.

Garrett: Your experience wasn’t even a misread; that’s a flaw in the error. The math you used—we don’t need to debate it, but what I would articulate is that doesn’t express the false positive rate, which is actually what you should be worried about. A false positive rate would say we read a license plate, FEDER, we’re confident it’s FEDER, and it’s stolen according to NCIC, so we send an alert.

It’s not just a function of how accurate we are, but how confident in our accuracy. There’s an important detail in how the system works, because technology will never be perfect, just like human eyes aren’t perfect. The question is what redundancies and what guardrails are you building into the system to prevent and reduce the likelihood of something bad happening.

In our case, let’s say it’s FEDER, and we’re 99% confident it’s an F, 99% on an E, 99% on a D, 99% on an E, and we’re only 80% confident that R is an R. We don’t send the alert.

Joel: Is that how it’s set up today?

Garrett: Yes, that’s how it works today. That’s an important detail because we will save that image, and we will store that under a certain confidence interval, but there is a very high bar for us to notify a local law enforcement officer in their MDT, in their patrol vehicle, of an NCIC alert. We have to be very confident, because even though we do the training and say you need to human verify this, and even though we do the training and say you need to double-check NCIC that there’s an active warrant, even though we do all that training, we know that humans are going to make mistakes.

We know that for many people, myself and yourself included, being pulled over by an officer is scary. It is. I’ve been pulled over before, I’ve sped, it happens. It’s scary, your heart races. We want to put that at a 0% likelihood that there is a wrongful traffic stop.

Joel: What’s the threshold? You said 80%, 99%. What’s the threshold that it has to be?

Garrett: I don’t think the number matters as much, because if I told you it’s 50%, you’d say, “What does that mean?” Here’s a way to think about it: It’s less than one in a million alerts that an officer says, “I’m not sure if that’s right.” Less than one in a million. To me, it’s incredibly low. Now, should it be one in a billion? Sure, that’s an interesting tradeoff.

For me, to your point, I want the OCR or the character recognition to be as good as possible. I would argue we have the best license plate reading camera in the world. We definitely are the largest provider of it in the world, so we probably have the best. For me, I think we’ve built these multiple redundancies to prevent—your situation is hard because I can’t control NCIC. What I can control is a wrongful traffic stop due to an OCR misread, and that I think we do have a lot of control over.

Joel: That’s a great transition to some broader questions about where we are today, what’s happening, and where we go in the future. I’d like to start with the future. You’re the man behind Flock. You founded it, you’re in charge of it, you’re the CEO. What is your vision for the future?

For context, I live in Plymouth, Minnesota. There are 18 cameras in Plymouth right now; that’s not every street corner today. Now, there are cities that have a lot more than that, and cities that have a lot less. My question is, what’s your vision for the future? Is there a Flock camera on every street corner, in every school? I know you guys are introducing new technology that’s not just cameras on top of streetlights. What’s your vision for the future, where are we going?

Garrett: One, thank you for the chance to talk about this, because I’ve spent the last decade of my life thinking about this. Just like you, I’m a father of three kids. My primary objective as a father is to keep them safe. They’ve got to be safe. Then I’ve got to make sure they’re educated, that they’re good people, productive members of society. But if they’re not safe, everything else starts to crumble. I think that’s true for a lot of kids. That lack of feeling safe starts to lead to these erosions of society.

If I zoom all the way out, we’ve always thought about crime and safety in two big buckets. You’ve got one bucket, which is emotional crime—crimes of passion. I hate to say it, we’re not going to stop those. They’ve been around for thousands of years. However long humans have been around, we have unfortunately been having passionate crimes, which is horrible. So we’ve got to solve those, but we’re not going to stop them.

The opportunistic crime, though—that’s actually very controllable. The majority of crime, let’s call it 95% to 99% of crime, is truly opportunistic. “I walk by your car, I believe I can get away with stealing it, so I choose to steal it.” That is the thought process.

What we’ve noticed is in certain places like San Francisco, four years ago, you could get away with almost any crime. Then two or three years ago, Mayor Breed and Mayor Lurie said, “Flock, we need help. It’s too easy to be a criminal, and our businesses are leaving, our people are leaving. This isn’t working for us.”

We deployed hundreds of license plate readers, we deployed our drones, we deployed our real-time crime center software to make officers more efficient. Now it’s one of the safest cities in America. Mayor Lurie has one of the highest approval ratings of any major city mayor—he might actually have the highest, last I checked.

For me, the future is a future where more cities look like San Francisco, where crime is incredibly hard to get away with—so hard that people just choose not to do it. That might seem like a distant future, but it’s happening in San Francisco. I think we’re going to do the same thing in Oakland. We’re in 7,000 cities today, and I’d like to get us to all 17,000 cities in America and create that future, because it’s quite doable. Whatever technology we need to build to help get there while maintaining our local societal norms is what we’re planning to do. That might sound crazy, but I said it 10 years ago, and now it’s really happening at scale. It’s a pretty exciting time.

Joel: Societal norms—you mentioned that. I want to be very clear, we’re not a political podcast, that’s not where we’re going to go, and I don’t really want to get into that here on the podcast. But societal norms—at one end of the spectrum, we’ve got people that are like, “If we have these on every corner, we’re going to have a dragnet map of your life without a warrant, and a Fourth Amendment violation.” Where do you fall on this whole topic of where Flock sits today, where the company sits tomorrow as you expand, and the warrantless Fourth Amendment concern—people’s concern of you doing a digital map of their entire life without a warrant?

Garrett: People tend to have three concerns or three questions about the company: privacy, constitutionality, and accountability.

You mentioned the constitutional one. That one’s pretty cut and dry. You and I don’t get to pick what’s a constitutional violation and what’s not. We have judges, we have elected officials, there’s a process for that. We follow the law, we follow the Constitution. So far, in our belief and what will be for a long time, the courts have deemed this is not a warrantless search; this is a valid product as it relates to the Fourth Amendment. So I don’t see any change there.

On the privacy one, though, there’s some real questions that we ask as well. Here’s a good example: Before I started Flock, this type of ALPR data was stored in perpetuity. It was resold for commercial purposes by repo trucks to insurance providers. It was pretty nasty, in my opinion. We were one of the first companies to say there’s going to be a 30-day default retention, and we aren’t going to sell the data.

I’ll tell you an interesting stat: We solved just over a million crimes last year on the Flock system in partnership with local law enforcement. If I told you that if we reduce the 30-day retention to 14 days, 30% fewer crimes would be solved—so roughly 300,000 more victims without justice—would you make that tradeoff?

Before you answer—I won’t make you answer that one on the spot—my point would be you and I shouldn’t pick. Actually, the Mayor of Plymouth and the City Council should make that decision, because that’s a fair tradeoff. We elect people who we believe match our values to make these very difficult, non-black-and-white questions. There’s no answer there, because you could go down with something like Flock and say, “We like the idea of Flock, but we only want to focus on Amber Alerts and Silver Alerts.” So there’s zero retention of the data, just alerts. I’d say, “Okay, you’re going to get about 50% of the value of the system, but if that’s what you want in Plymouth, great, we’d love to help you, but you’re still going to be safer.” Now, you’re going to be less safe than San Francisco, but that’s an option.

For us, we don’t want to push our opinion as individual citizens. I live in Atlanta, you live in Plymouth. We just wish that more elected officials would do their research, do their homework, form an opinion, engage the community, and then set a standard that makes sense for them.

Joel: Let’s go down the elected officials route; this was actually one of my questions. I’ve seen Congress members—not one, not two, a couple of them now—post on Instagram about introducing bills that would withhold federal funding from municipalities that would use Flock. I’m curious what you make of that. None of these, by the way, to my knowledge, have been introduced as of the time of this recording; they’ve all just been discussions, but they’re being thrown out there. It is being talked about.

Garrett: At the highest level, nothing would make me happier than if we had state-by-state regulation on this type of technology. That to me is so crystal clear, because the lack of regulation on this type of technology just shows that our elected officials need to move faster than they have historically. I’m not the first person to say that. That’s the case with technology in general, where we just tend to build and innovate as a country faster than we can regulate. That’s generally okay, but in this case, they’re behind.

The proposition of federal defunding of roughly, in this case, 80% of police departments because they use technology to keep their community safe is completely… I don’t know how that’s logical to people when there are so many better alternatives to regulation.

I think that there is a very low likelihood that anyone is that irresponsible to even propose such legislation. When it has been discussed in the past—which was about six months ago—it barely made it out of someone’s mouth before it was killed. I would just challenge those Congress folks, men and women, instead of being critical of the men and women who work tirelessly to keep us safe and the tools they need to be effective, maybe we should actually just talk about what guardrails are necessary for everyone to feel good about what’s required.

To me—and Joel, I don’t know if you agree, I hope you do—I think it’s crazy that in America today, there’s a 50/50 chance of getting away with homicide. That seems completely unacceptable as a society. Banning tools that allow us to drive clearance rates higher…

I say this because in Atlanta, where I live, there was a woman who was violently murdered in the middle of the night in Piedmont Park, our biggest park, five years ago, and that case is still cold. You know why? Because even though there were cameras, the cameras weren’t working. If those cameras were working, that woman’s family would have justice. They don’t today, and I think that’s horrible. We should not be comfortable with that as a society, and I know in Atlanta we are not.

Joel: We talked about Congressmen and elected politicians. I have to get your viewpoint on what you make of the public pushback, or towns canceling contracts, or not renewing contracts. By the way, I want to be clear on the podcast, I actually felt there was a lot of miss and/or shoddy reporting on a couple of the towns that “canceled” contracts, because they actually were set to expire and didn’t get renewed, and I dug into that. As a journalist, it irked me. But that’s not the point.

I am curious, what’s your viewpoint on the public pushback, towns either canceling or not renewing contracts? Flock’s not something that people use; it’s not something I use. It’s not something I’m opting into like iCloud or whatever, it’s something you have to accept, because you’re driving down the road and I didn’t opt into it like I do with my AirPods or my phone. I’m guessing that’s kind of some of the public pushback here when we were talking about the whole map and dragnet. We discussed your take on that, but I’m curious about your viewpoint on this public pushback and towns canceling or not renewing contracts.

Garrett: It’s a really interesting phenomenon, because in most businesses—I’ll take the case of your business—if one of your advertisers or one of your partners chooses not to renew, it’s not a headline. When you add a new advertiser, it’s not a headline. It’s been interesting because we’ve added probably 10 times the number of customers that are new than who have not renewed their service in the last 90 days, but you won’t read that in the headlines, right? Because it’s not an interesting story to say, “Oh, this city adopted Flock.” It’s only interesting to say, “This city has paused their service” or canceled it.

What’s also interesting to me is the media hasn’t reported on the dozens of agencies who paused their service, saw crime go up, and have now turned them back on. It’s just interesting. I don’t know why, but to your point, some are turning it off, and that’s their choice. What they will find is they will be less safe, and then they will call us back, whether it’s in a week, 30 days, or a year. We have a demonstrable impact on public safety, and some cities have tried the experiment and it fails, and they have an obligation to keep their citizens safe.

Joel: Final question before we go into a hot round of however long we have left: You’re a private company, and you’re the middleman between the public and the government. You’re helping the police, but you’re not a supplier, you’re a service. You’re selling a service, it’s a SaaS. It’s a subscription service, and if they stop paying, like we just discussed, you turn it off; they no longer have access to the service. But it’s a service to the government, but you’re serving the government in between the public, because you’re taking pictures of the public’s license plates or whoever’s running through, and then it’s going to the government. You’re not a government-owned entity. It’s not a common place thing in this type of situation.

Garrett: This is a really interesting question, so it gives me a chance to hit on a few points. One, and this has been misreported as well—hopefully you can help me get this word out—we do not own the data, the government owns the data. We don’t have access to it. We are the custodian, and the reason why we did this goes back to my example.

We got questions from our customers like, “We’re used to just buying equipment.” I said, “Well, how’s that going for you? Are you experts in camera installation, camera maintenance?” My Atlanta example before is a prime example of what happens when we ask our government to do too much. Law enforcement is really good at one thing, which is hopefully solving crime. That’s what we ask them to do. They’re not necessarily good at building cameras, designing cameras.

It’s important to know our customer owns the data. I would actually agree with you, one of the hardest parts about building this business is that the last company to go public in this space was 25 years ago. That’s not every measure for success by any means—you can build a great business that doesn’t go public—but when you think about other industries that have seen the sheer benefit of technology, we’ve left behind local government. No one wants to service local government.

This is one of the reasons why, as you and I talked about, this is a controversial company. I appreciate that. We are not setting up the next generation of entrepreneurs to get excited about working with local government when, honestly, they need more innovation, local government needs more technology. It’s hard, it’s really hard, but I think it’s worth it.

Joel: Let me ask you—Josh and I, if anyone’s cutting in now and hasn’t heard this, Josh is the Chief Communications Officer I talked to, and he’s been in a couple of our stories—he did make a mention of something you just noted, that you guys don’t own the data, it’s stored on AWS (Amazon Web Services), and that it’s bucketed by municipalities, and certain municipalities can have sharing with other municipalities.

We see in the news countless examples of whether it’s in Texas, or your home area, Georgia—bad actors, bad police misusing your system, stalking women, stalking ex-girlfriends and their family members, checking a certain license plate 179 times in a certain period of time, etc. Obviously, there are audit logs—Josh told me about this and this is how people get caught with audit logs.

I am curious, do you guys have multi-factor authentication? The reason I ask this is because even my iCloud and my Meta accounts have multi-factor authentication, and it makes it easier to track who that actual person is in the audit log and the audit trail to get caught. Does that make sense?

Garrett: Yes, so let’s hit on a few of these. As a matter of fact, we do. We do require multi-factor authentication, which is a step in the right direction. We’ve had that for years. Now, we used to not require it, it used to be optional, and the main reason why being if you’re a town of 10 sworn officers, you’re unlikely to be offering both a laptop and a mobile device that are government-issued. To do proper multi-factor authentication, you need to have multiple devices.

We’ve evolved our thinking and said any version of MFA is better than no MFA, so we will just mandate it now, which we’ve now done.

To your point on auditability and accountability, yeah, I actually think this is a problem more broadly in law enforcement—that we’re one of the only systems that actually has auditing and has abnormal behavior detection in it. All these cases you see happening are because our system is flagging, “That’s pretty weird.” It’s not necessarily illegal—innocent until proven guilty—but a criminal investigation should have occurred. I wish more state regulations pushed that every system law enforcement uses needed to have this level of sophisticated auditing and abnormal detection.

We’ve got to do more there. The only other point I’d add, Joel, is I was just earlier today on the phone with one of our customers in Ohio, and they were sharing a success story on an ICAC crime—Internet Crimes Against Children. Let’s think about society, let’s think at the bottom of society, some of the most evil people. He was sharing with me this story of how the case was completely cold, but then they were using Flock and they found the individual, they’ve arrested him. You’re not going to go to the 5:00 news and talk about an ICAC case; it’s not appropriate, people don’t want to hear about this stuff.

I have the benefit of hearing from my customers every single day of these incredibly heroic stories where they found that one needle in the haystack. I wish the media and I wish our customers did an even better job of selling that story, but I also can appreciate that as a society, we don’t want to hear about all the evil that’s out there, and we rely on local law enforcement to catch those bad people, and state law enforcement and federal law enforcement to catch those bad people.

The abuse is a problem. We need to continue to get that down to zero. Any level of abuse is unacceptable, to be very clear, but I don’t think we should miss the fact that over a million cases were solved last year with this technology, and the level of abuse is incredibly low relative to that.

Joel: I would be remiss—this was not in my original rundown, but I know you’re in the news all the time, you are, and Flock is as well. The fact that we’re sitting here and that we were brought together because of my situation that I experienced, I’m sure in the comments on the internet, people would skewer me if I did not ask the question.

Weeks ago—the last month’s kind of a blur with everything that’s happened—weeks ago, a journalist asked you a question about what you make of the people that are cutting down, shooting, etc., the Flock cameras. You gave a passionate response that used the word “domestic terrorists” or something like that. I know since then you’ve apologized for it, I’ve seen that video as well and that coverage. If we went back in time, I have to ask about it.

Garrett: Look, I clearly could have done a better job delineating between individuals who commit felonies—where, to be clear, destruction of government property, destruction of property, is a felony in many states. We can change the law, but currently the law says that if you vandalize something, that’s illegal. To individuals that are promoting breaking the law, I just find that confusing. We’re a company that, by and large, by design from our founding, was that people shouldn’t break the law. I don’t know why that’s controversial, that I don’t agree with breaking the law.

Now, what I got wrong, and what I apologized for to your point, a comment that I made 18 months ago, was not clearly separating that viewpoint from organizations like the ACLU or the EFF, and now groups like DeFlock, who are trying to make sure their voice is heard. I think that’s great. We might disagree on some of the details, but I think that’s perfectly fine. Just like I have a right as a business owner, as a father, to share my voice, to vote, to do that—I think that’s great.

I didn’t delineate that enough, and I should have been clearer that I think committing a felony is bad, and I think voicing your opinion is A-OK, it’s great. I actually think the more of it, the better. I think people should be more involved in local politics. I don’t know what your level of engagement is in Plymouth, but I can tell you that you have an ability to influence what’s happening, and it also impacts your life more than you think than state and federal politics.

Joel: I really appreciate your time. I really appreciate your team setting this up, I appreciate you coming on the podcast. You’re definitely welcome to come back. I would love to continue the conversation another time in the future. I think there’s so much more that you and I could talk about in terms of technology, what your company can do, what other companies are doing, the differentiation points, and I’d welcome the opportunity.

Garrett: Awesome, awesome. Thank you very much, appreciate it, and we’ll talk to you soon.

fullText:
Roadside safety advocates say some automated license plate readers may not meet highway safety standards

Flock Safety cameras have been pilloried for facilitating the AI-powered surveillance of private citizens and for targeting immigrants for years. But now safety advocates are also claiming that their physical location can pose potential roadside hazards.

At the bottom of a tree-lined hill on a narrow, two lane rural road in Greene county, Ohio, stands a black metal rod with a camera and solar panel attached at the top.

The camera, an automated license plate reader (ALPR), is owned by Flock Safety and is painted black, making it difficult to see.

Its dark color isn’t the only thing that makes it a potential hazard for drivers.

The metal rod has no breakaway plate – a safety feature close to the ground that, in the case of a collision with a vehicle, sees the pole snap, reducing the resistance and impact experienced by the vehicle and the people inside it.

It has no obvious stickers indicating it’s been inspected by safety authorities and is placed about two feet from the edge of the asphalt road. According to the Ohio department of transportation (ODOT), however, “On uncurbed facilities, [license plate readers must be] at least 8 [feet] from the nearest edge of a travel lane.”

The Beavercreek police department, Flock’s customer in this case, says that Flock is responsible for all instalments and that all cameras in its jurisdiction “received the appropriate approval”.

ALPRs record license plate details, as well as the make, model, color and any other notable features of a vehicle. Flock has an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 cameras deployed in more than 6,000 communities across the US. (Flock told the Guardian it wouldn’t share the exact number or location of its surveillance devices.)

This potential physical danger is one that Tennessee-based Steve Eimers, known online as the Guardrail Guy, has found himself increasingly documenting in recent months. Following the death of his 17-year-old daughter after the vehicle in which she was traveling crashed into a roadside structure on Interstate 75 a decade ago, Eimers has toured the country to highlight the failure of various authorities to meet their own legal requirements. His videos, posted across social media, have garnered millions of views.

“There are a billion different people looking into the top part of the cameras [but] nobody’s been looking at the bottom, and the crashworthy elements,” he says.

“The guardrail had to go through a heavy vetting process – they had to do a whole series of crash tests, they had to submit the crash test results in full with photos [which] are reviewed by state [department of transportation] engineers,” he says.

In 2024, crashes between a motor vehicle and a fixed barrier accounted for 26% of vehicle deaths nationwide, according to the National Safety Council, a non-profit.

According to the Federal Highway Administration, sign poles and rods can become a deadly hazard for motorists, which has led to the establishment of a standard “that requires all roadside sign supports in the clear zone … to be breakaway, yielding, or shielded by a barrier or crash cushion”.

Roadside safety hardware includes crash cushions, breakaway supports, transitions and other structures and spaces that help to prevent catastrophe for motorists who leave the road.

“Permits are required when working within ODOT’s right-of-way, including the installation of license plate reader cameras,” says David Rose, of Ohio’s department of transportation, who notes that state authorities are not involved in the installation of ALPRs, even when located on the state’s right-of-way.

“All work performed within corporation limits must be approved through the appropriate city or village, as ODOT does not have jurisdiction within corporation limits.”

Eimers says he has only ever found one Flock pole, in Erie county, Ohio, installed with the required breakaway plate.

But even in that case, he says the breakaway plate was positioned higher off the ground than the Federal Highway Administration permits, meaning the metal pole could catch the underside of a low-lying vehicle and potentially ignite a battery- or gas-fueled fire.

“Flock is not a sophisticated user of roadside safety hardware. They are nowhere near doing what they are supposed to be, what should be done,” Eimers says.

Flock and police departments say the cameras are an effective crime reduction tool, having played a key role in recovering stolen property and missing persons across the country.

The company says it follows all state and local requirements when it comes to the safe location of its hardware.

“We do not agree with the premise that Flock regularly installs poles in violation of federal, state, or local safety requirements. The appropriate pole type and installation specifications depend on the roadway, speed, location, jurisdiction, and requirements of the relevant transportation or permitting authority,” says Paris Lewbel, a Flock Safety spokesperson, who noted that the company planned to undergo a review of camera pole installations across its network.

“Customers generally determine camera locations based on their public safety priorities. Flock then works with the customer.”

Flock isn’t alone. ALPR companies such as Motorola Solutions, Redflex Traffic Systems and others are apparently routinely failing to meet roadside structure requirements, including often using other structures to place their monitoring devices on, in violation of state requirements.

While in urban areas Flock cameras are oftentimes attached high up on traffic lights or other larger structures, reducing the crash risk, in suburban and rural areas – where traffic speeds are typically higher – they are regularly erected as stand-alone structures where they add to the number of objects drivers can collide with.

What Eimers and others have found is that Flock and other ALPR camera structures, for the most part, are not being inspected by municipal authorities for meeting safety requirements as other roadside structures such as municipal signs are. What’s more, that they are painted black, with no reflecting surfaces, can make them difficult for drivers to see at night.

“Without that, what can happen is that metal pipe can act like a spear; that’s hollow pipe, it’ll core out your brain,’ warns Eimers, a registered nurse who says he has spent tens of thousands of hours inspecting and researching roadside safety requirements and manuals since his daughter’s death.

“We know that a lot of people leave the road, so we want a forgiving roadside.”

title: Honor Magic V6 review: sleek foldable phone lacking a bit of polish
description:
Super-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by software
Honor’s svelte Android phone-tablet has been given a glow-up for its sixth version, offering a great alternative to Samsung for a fancy foldable with a red suede-like back framed in gold.
The Magic V6 continues the Chinese challenger brand’s strategy of taking a razor-thin device and slapping a giant circular lump on the back to fit in top-class cameras, something others often forgo. It costs a not inconsiderable £1,500 (€1,700/A$2,999) but only until August when the price jumps to a cool £2,000 (€2,300) – a solid £300 more than last year’s model as the cost of RAMageddon continues to bite, even at the very top end of the market.

The Magic V6 continues the Chinese challenger brand’s strategy of taking a razor-thin device and slapping a giant circular lump on the back to fit in top-class cameras, something others often forgo. It costs a not inconsiderable £1,500 (€1,700/A$2,999) but only until August when the price jumps to a cool £2,000 (€2,300) – a solid £300 more than last year’s model as the cost of RAMageddon continues to bite, even at the very top end of the market.

Other than a new red-backed version, the Magic V6 is almost indistinguishable from the great V5 from last year. It is one of the thinnest and lightest foldable tablets on the market, has a great fingerprint scanner in the power button and has a proper IP68 water resistance rating matching the best slab phones, making it easy to use as a daily driver. When closed it handles just like a regular flagship Android phone with a great, crisp and smooth OLED display.

Once opened, the internal screen is one of the best available, ready for all your media-watching or multitasking needs. But the crease down the middle that allows the screen to fold is slightly more noticeable than some rivals and the integrated screen film is a fingerprint magnet, so it will need cleaning regularly to make the best of it.

Main screen: 7.95in (403ppi) 120Hz OLED flexible display

Cover screen: 6.52in (406ppi) 120Hz OLED

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5

Operating system: MagicOS 10 (Android 16)

Camera: 50MP + 50MP ultrawide + 64MP 3x tele; 2x 20MP selfie

Connectivity: 5G, dual sim + esim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, GNSS

Water resistance: IP68/69 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)

Dimensions folded: 156.7 x 74.5 x 8.75-9mm

Dimensions unfolded: 156.7 x 145.6 x 4.0-4.1mm

The Magic V6 has Qualcomm’s top Android chip for 2026, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, making it one of the best performers on the market, rivalling top slab phones such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.

However, by default the Magic V6 uses a “balanced” battery mode, which significantly inhibits the phone’s top performance. It isn’t noticeable in day-to-day messaging and browsing but it was in games and other high-intensity tasks. Switching the phone to its “performance” battery mode significantly improved things at the expense of heat and battery life.

The Honor has a very large battery compared with most foldable phone rivals, which helps it last almost two full days between charges while actively using a mixture of the screens for more than eight hours for general browsing, messaging, work and media consumption. Playing games drains the battery a bit faster but the Magic V6 should outlast even the heaviest of usage days.

The phone runs Honor’s version of last year’s Android 16, MagicOS 10, which means it isn’t as up to date as some rivals running Android 17. Honor will provide seven years of Android version and security updates for devices sold within Europe.

MagicOS has improved since last year. It looks quite nice, has plenty of customisation options and tools for making the most of the folding screen, including the excellent ability to split-screen three apps beyond the bounds of the physical display, which was introduced last year.

Various AI tools are strewn throughout the operating system, including Google’s Gemini, which you can set to open in split-screen next to whatever app you are using at the time by quickly flexing the tablet. Many of the tools work as shortcuts for performing tasks such as saving screenshots, editing photos and changing settings on your phone.

The “AI button” is meant to launch actions such as turning on the torch or opening an AI tool by double-tapping, though not depressing, the power button, but it doesn’t work. There are various other parts of the operating system that are unpolished. A bug prevents Google’s Chrome browser from opening in split-screen. Apps that are out of date are described as having a “low version” by Honor’s App Market, which also insists on trying to update apps installed from Google Play, bringing the two app stores into conflict. The Honor lacks the ability to have a different home screen layout for the inside and outside screens, and messaging apps such as WhatsApp routinely insist on opening as small floating windows if you tap a message notification, even on the outside screen.

These little niggles could be overlooked on a significantly cheaper phone, but not on a £1,500-£2,000 device. You can and should expect better.

The enormous circular bump on the back houses three cameras, with a 20MP selfie camera in each of the two screens for a total of five cameras.

The cameras have changed little since last year’s V5 and perform very similarly. The main 50MP camera shoots great photos at 12MP as standard with good detail and range with its cropped 2x zoom, though it can notably suffer from moiré on stripped textures. The 50MP ultra wide camera has been improved since the V5, solving some of the distortion problems. The 64MP 3x telephoto is the best of the bunch, capturing excellent detail, even with its 2x crop zoom for an effective 6x magnification. Its digital zoom remains good to 30x before becoming obviously blown up.

Low light photography is pretty good across all the lenses, while the camera app has tons of features, including many AI tools and a good manual mode for more creative photography. The Magic V6 shoots decent video up to 4K at 60 frames a second and can be used in various partly folded orientations.

The battery will maintain at least 80% capacity after 1,200 full-charge cycles. The phone is generally repairable and Honor publishes pricing for spare parts, including £609 for an internal screen and £152 for the external screen, plus labour and shipping. Honor offers a free screen repair (Care+) for 24 months if bought before 2 August.

The device contains limited recycled materials, which Honor breaks down in the phone’s environmental impact report. The company offers trade-in and refurbished products.

The Honor Magic V6 has an introductory price of £1,499.99 (€1,699.90/A$2,999), which will increase to £1,999.99 (€2,299.90) from August 2026 in some regions.

For comparison, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899 and the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold costs £1,749.

The Magic V6 is another very attractive book-style foldable from Honor, but it fails to move things on from last year in an increasingly competitive category.

It has really great battery life, matching some of the best slab phones. The outside screen is great, while the inside screen is good but has a more visible crease than some recent rivals. The Magic V6 feels particularly good when used as a phone, while the massive bump fits in some great cameras and means it doesn’t rock around on a table like some others.

But it is the software that continues to let Honor down. It just isn’t as up to date or polished as it needs to be on a device this expensive.

As good as the Magic V6 is, it lacks a compelling reason to buy it over more complete rivals from Samsung, Google and others.

Pros: slim, light, just like a normal phone when closed, great performance, very long battery life, good internal screen, decent camera, good fingerprint scanner, IP68/9 water and dust resistance rating.

Cons: very expensive, software not as refined as needed, more fragile than a regular device, costly to repair, not much of an upgrade on previous model.

title: Inside the growing vigilante movement to knock out Flock surveillance cameras
description:
An underground network of privacy activists is disabling or destroying the ubiquitous surveillance devices sprouting up across the US
The first time that “NoMark” tried to knock out a Flock camera feed, he waited an hour for the perfect moment – pacing in and out of bushes that towered over him, a few feet behind a pole holding up the device.
“I was just so nervous,” he said.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
The first time that “NoMark” tried to knock out a Flock camera feed, he waited an hour for the perfect moment – pacing in and out of bushes that towered over him, a few feet behind a pole holding up the device.

“I was just so nervous,” he said.

NoMark, as he’s known on Instagram, had already gained an online following of hundreds of thousands for posting videos of himself wearing a black mask and taking on small-time vigilante missions: breaking up fights outside a bar and breaking into a refinery he believed was “polluting the city real bad”. The Minnesota Star Tribune dubbed him “Minneapolis’ Batman”. He spoke to the Guardian under condition of anonymity to discuss potentially illegal acts.

On this June night, he set his sights on a new target: automated license plate readers (ALPRs) made by the US company Flock Safety.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

These black cameras, which are hooked up to a rectangular solar panel and typically mounted on a pole, snap photos of passing vehicles and run the pictures against large databases. They have sparked nationwide backlash from pro-privacy critics, who point to public records suggesting that these devices can help law enforcement keep tabs on specific license plates and the people driving these cars. That they can sweep in so many people’s location from an innocent act in a public space – regardless of whether the target is a suspect in a crime, and without a warrant – has led to fears of mass surveillance.

Flock, based in Georgia and valued at $8.4bn, says its cameras scan license plates billions of times each month in about 6,000 communities in nearly every state in the US.

The company said in a February blogpost that its ALPRs are “not mass surveillance tools” and that it “cannot track vehicles, much less individual people”.

Across the street from a Taco Bell, NoMark couldn’t stop thinking about whether he would get caught, and the adrenaline felt paralyzing – even though this felt “on brand” for his online persona, which has won him more than 700,000 followers on Instagram and TikTok. After a few minutes of not spotting any cars on the road, he climbed a few feet up the pole, taped up the camera to block its lens and snipped the wires that powered the whole operation. Then he ended his phone’s recording and fled.

Nowadays, NoMark is much calmer on these excursions, and it only takes him a few minutes to get the job done after having taken down more than a dozen cameras, he says. But he still assumes the police are looking for him. Even if he does get arrested, he’s hopeful the charges won’t be too severe – and more important, he “just wants to send a message”.

“I’m not afraid to do things if I think they’re right,” he says. “These things are coming up so fast across the country that this is kind of the only way to combat them.”

The Minneapolis camera destroyer is not alone. As anger grows towards law enforcement contracts with Flock, vigilantes across the country are taking matters into their own hands by smashing, obstructing or taking down these cameras. Many are leaning into their creative side: “paint bombing” the devices, planting American flags at the scene after damaging them, 3D printing objects to help obstruct the camera’s view and leaving colorful messages like “hahaha get wrecked ya surveilling fucks”. Some influencers are even creating fake cease-and-desist letters from Flock, capitalizing on the company’s negative public perception.

The Guardian has identified at least 33 instances of people damaging, vandalizing and destroying Flock cameras, across 23 states, that appear to have the explicit message of protesting surveillance.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Flock, along with police departments across the US, say these cameras are integral for public safety, and capture vehicle details that can help in investigations, such as license plate numbers and the make and model of vehicles. Flock’s website also advertises how these cameras can “stop crime in real time” by alerting officers “the moment a suspect car passes by” – suggesting that cops can act quickly on these leads to pursue a target. The company’s CEO, Garrett Langley, has described some pro-privacy critics as wanting to “normalize lawlessness” and “weaken public safety”.

NoMark has not been caught in his campaign against Flock cameras. Others are facing charges. Jeffrey Sovern in Suffolk, Virginia, has been charged with destruction of property for allegedly damaging more than a dozen Flock cameras. Sovern has not admitted to the act but did tell police that he finds these cameras to be unconstitutional.

He wrote on a GoFundMe created to pay for legal expenses: “I will take the silver lining that this can be a catalyst in a bigger movement to roll back intrusive surveillance.”

A handful of other cases have drawn criminal charges, too. In New Mexico, Jevon Martinez was arrested after allegedly destroying 13 Flock cameras.

When asked if he would “continue to take down these Flock cameras”, Martinez told local news station KRQE: “Absolutely. They are a clear and present threat to public safety.” The news outlet also reported that a sign near one of the damaged Flock cameras read: “You’re welcome, the Republic of New Mexico.”

Flock did not comment on vigilantes knocking out its cameras but did publish a blogpost in mid-July about helping government agencies respond if a camera is damaged.

“We’ve planned for it,” the company wrote, adding that protection plans are available for purchase.

Law enforcement is aware of the backlash and responding. Dozens of state fusion centers – collaborative hubs where federal and local agencies share intelligence about crime and terrorism – circulated memos across law enforcement agencies this summer directing officers to monitor anti-Flock advocacy as part of a directive to protect national security, according to reporting from journalist Dan Boguslaw. One report Boguslaw obtained from a Wisconsin intelligence agency calls for increased vigilance and patrols during protests and events such as a “national week of action” in mid-August. That intelligence digest also advised local law enforcement to report “vandalism, disruption or sabotage” of ALPRs to fusion centers.

The winds of sympathy online are not blowing in Flock’s favor. News articles and videos about vigilantes’ cases have drawn support from online commenters, who post made-up, neighborly alibis like seeing accused parties rescuing dogs or serving meals at a soup kitchen at the time a camera was destroyed.

The anti-Flock online ecosystem also features an exchange of tips and strategies for kneecapping the cameras. One Reddit poster shared a 3D print file for an object he says can help block cameras without damaging them or violating vandalism laws.

NoMark, in Minneapolis, says he receives dozens of messages daily from people wanting to help, letting him know they’re taking similar actions or asking for advice on staying safe. He keeps his replies vague, as he doesn’t want his words to get people arrested. He tells those writing to him to avoid driving past the cameras, and to make sure they’re going out late at night when they no one else is around. He reiterates that they should cover up completely, including their face and hands.

He also tells them: “Always cover the camera.”

Minneapolis’s Batman thinks you need both political pressure on elected officials and vigilantism to achieve change. He believes showing up to city council meetings – and he’s shown up to a few without his mask – is helpful but “it does obviously take time, and it’s not always effective”.

“The more time you take, the more data they get on people,” he said.

More than 80 cities have disbanded, decided not to renew or rejected contracts with Flock in recent years, or deactivated the company’s cameras, including Austin and Denver, although activists remain concerned about the devices’ continued use in those areas.

Beyond general surveillance creep, privacy advocates fear US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s ability to access these camera feeds through legal loopholes to pursue immigrants.

Police officers have used the cameras for their own personal ends as well. Several have lost their jobs after misusing the devices to stalk people. Though license plate reading is the cameras’ bread and butter, 404 Media reported last week that cops have used Flock’s search feature to look for people with distinct markers – like tattoos and specific T-shirts – and not just cars.

Congress is taking note, and earlier this month a Texas lawmaker introduced a bill requiring warrants for data collected by Flock cameras.

Not all anti-Flock activism takes the form of camera destruction. A crowdsourced map created by the grassroots group DeFlock maps out more than 115,000 ALPRs across the country. The organization’s site also allows users to see if their license plates have been searched in Flock’s system, get directions to avoid ALPRs and find upcoming meetings about municipal Flock contracts.

Flock’s CEO has taken note of DeFlock’s advocacy, too, and characterized the organization as “terroristic” but recently apologized for that label. In a tweet, he attributed DeFlock’s popularity to his company’s “inadequate response to the questions and concerns that people have about ALPR”. The company is adapting to the backlash, canceling an always-on recording feature, “human distress detection”, which was intended to detect screaming.

A local chapter of DeFlock, in Norfolk, Virginia, says it does not endorse vigilantes targeting Flock cameras but does not advocate against it, either.

The Virginia chapter is working to ensure the city either cancels or does not renew its contract with Flock, but so far it hasn’t had success, and members are particularly angry about speaking restrictions on the topic. At a city council meeting last month, the mayor enforced a rule about reducing repetitive comments to limit the number of speakers who wanted to share their concerns about Flock, the Virginian-Pilot reported.

“We recognize it’s the inevitable outcome of a system designed to prevent people’s voices from being heard,” said a DeFlock spokesperson.

title: ICE officers to wear body cameras during vehicle stops, border czar says
description: In the wake of multiple fatal shootings involving U.S.
fullText:
July 19 (Reuters) - In the wake of multiple fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, the agency will require its officers to record ‌vehicle stops with at least one body camera, Trump administration border czar Tom Homan ‌said Sunday.

"They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want ​the American people to see what the officers saw when they took that action," Homan said on the "Fox & Friends Weekend" program.

Homan's comments come after federal immigration agents fatally shot two men six days apart during traffic stops in Texas and Maine earlier this month. There is no body-camera footage from ICE agents involved ‌in those incidents.

In a separate ⁠interview on CBS' "Face the Nation" show, Homan said money for the cameras was held up during the partial government shutdown earlier this year.

"The cameras have been ⁠purchased right now," Homan said. "They're training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide."

The agency's tactics came under renewed public scrutiny in recent days after an ICE officer on July 13 killed a driver ​from Colombia ​in the coastal Maine town of Biddeford, about 15 ​miles (24 km) south of Portland. Six ‌days earlier, another ICE officer in Houston fatally shot a Mexican national.

Homan said last week the agency would temporarily suspend most vehicle stops around the country to review procedures. Within 24 hours of Homan's comments, U.S. President Donald Trump directed federal immigration agents to resume them.

The back-to-back shootings sparked protests in Maine, Houston and Boston and raised questions over ICE agents' lack of body cameras.

ICE launched ‌a body-camera pilot program in 2024 and deployed cameras ​to officers in five cities: Baltimore, Buffalo, Detroit, Philadelphia, and ​Washington, D.C.

The Trump administration moved last year ​to slow-walk the program, urging Congress to cut funding by 75%, Reuters reported ‌in January.

In February, after the killing of ​two U.S. citizens during ​an immigration crackdown in Minnesota, then U.S. Department of Homeland Security chief Kristi Noem said the body camera program would be rolled out to ICE agents nationwide "as funding is available."

At ​least seven people have been shot ‌dead during federal immigration enforcement operations since January 2025, when Trump launched mass deportations ​after returning to office following campaign promises of an immigration crackdown.

title: Democrat lawmaker's 107 mph traffic stop brings bodycam battle front and center again
description: The sheriff's office involved in a New Hampshire lawmaker's 107 mph traffic stop lacks body cameras and dashboard cameras due to funding shortfalls.
fullText:
A New Hampshire Democratic lawmaker's 107 mph traffic stop has thrust the debate over police body cameras and dashboard cameras back into the spotlight after Fox News Digital confirmed the sheriff's office involved in the stop has neither.

The lack of body camera and dashboard camera footage has become a focal point in the legal battle involving state Rep. Ellen Read, who is fighting charges stemming from two Rockingham County traffic stops, including one in which a deputy accused her of driving 107 mph. Read argues both stops violated a provision of the New Hampshire Constitution protecting lawmakers while traveling to and from legislative duties.

Without body camera or dashboard camera footage, there is no official recording of the traffic stop that sparked a constitutional fight over legislative immunity.

Maj. Christopher Bashaw of the Rockingham County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital the agency does not use body-worn cameras or dashboard cameras because it lacks funding to purchase them.

Dem Lawmaker Says Constitution Barred Police From Stopping Her After Alleged 100 Mph Speeding

"We don't have that either," Bashaw said when asked whether deputies use body cameras or dashboard cameras, adding the sheriff's office would like to equip deputies with the technology.

New Hampshire lawmakers established a Body-Worn and Dashboard Camera Fund in 2021 to provide matching grants to local law enforcement agencies for purchasing cameras and covering maintenance, replacement and data storage costs. All local law enforcement agencies are eligible to apply.

State law also requires agencies that choose to deploy body cameras to adopt policies governing when officers must record law enforcement encounters, including traffic stops. The law, however, does not require agencies to purchase or use body cameras.

Ice Resumes Nationwide Traffic Stops Under New Policy Requiring Body Cameras

It is unclear whether the Rockingham County Sheriff's Office has applied for funding through the state grant program.

Read told Fox News Digital she has consistently supported legislation governing body-worn cameras, as well as funding to help law enforcement agencies purchase them. She also said she would be willing to work with the Rockingham County Sheriff's Office to help secure funding for body cameras in the next state budget.

Read said she supports funding body cameras even though she questions other forms of law enforcement spending, including military-grade equipment and expensive vehicles.

She also disputed the sheriff's office's assertion that she recorded part of the traffic stop on her cellphone.

"They are incorrect, I wish I had," Read said. "The officers conveniently not wearing/using body cams are the reason that I'm investing in a dash cam."

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

According to Read, the sheriff's office misunderstood what happened during the stop. She said she did not record the encounter and that a witness listening during a cellphone call later testified in court.

Read has argued the constitutional provision protects lawmakers from being delayed while traveling to legislative duties – not from prosecution.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

"I admitted to the officer and in court that I was going about 85 miles an hour on the highway," she said, adding that she was willing to accept a speeding ticket but disputed the deputy's allegation that she was traveling 107 mph and driving recklessly.

Lawrence Friedman, a professor at New England Law, said the constitutional provision dates back centuries and was intended to prevent lawmakers from being delayed while performing their legislative duties – not to provide blanket immunity from traffic stops or criminal prosecution.

"I think it's probably not the case that this provision provides some kind of absolute immunity," Friedman told Fox News Digital. "It's unlikely that a court would say, 'No, you're absolutely immune from arrest for a moving violation that everyone else would be subject to arrest for just because you happen to be a legislator.'"

Friedman also said the New Hampshire Supreme Court's refusal to immediately hear Read's constitutional challenge should not be interpreted as a ruling on the merits of her argument.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"My understanding is that it's not that her appeal is denied," Friedman said. "The Supreme Court said no because they want to see how it plays out at the trial court."

Bashaw said the constitutional provision was intended to prevent law enforcement from interfering with legislative business, not to shield lawmakers from accountability for dangerous driving.

"The claim that you're immune from all types of arrests... that'd be like saying you could drive at those speeds, commit a vehicular homicide, and that you are not allowed to be held accountable because you're traveling to and from session," Bashaw said.

Read acknowledged the constitutional language could be modernized while preserving its original intent.

"I did not write this constitutional provision... it was written before cars existed," she said.

title: Russia hacks doorbell cameras to spy on NATO bases
description: Civilian devices on military transport routes targeted to identify weapons sent to Ukraine
fullText:
Joe is based in Brussels, where he focuses on European politics and defence. He has covered the Ukraine war and its peace negotiations and reported on US elections from Washington DC

Russia has been spying on Nato military bases through civilian cameras connected to the internet, Dutch intelligence services said.

Kremlin-based hackers accessed the devices to monitor the transfer of military equipment to Ukraine, the AIVD domestic security and MIVD military intelligence agencies said.

Their joint investigation found the Russian operation had targeted cameras pointing towards military transport routes in the hope of identifying what weapons were being sent to Kyiv.

“Organisations with IP [internet protocol] cameras on these routes have now been warned so that they could take action,” the agencies warned after exposing what they described as a “large-scale Russian operation”.

They said it had targeted “European Nato member states, including the Netherlands, and Ukraine”.

Internet protocol cameras, which are cameras with internet access, have risen to prominence in recent years because of cheap Chinese imports and high-speed broadband connections.

While the intelligence agencies did not specify the type of cameras hacked, the doorbell systems are frequently used by people to monitor their property from mobile phones. Hackers then use readily available apps to scan for devices that might be accessible.

The Dutch investigation found that many of the cameras were unsecured, and “often have standard passwords, outdated firmware and standard configurations”.

They said: “When the IP camera is identified, the malicious party can attempt to access the IP camera via the internet. This is often relatively easy, because many IP cameras connected to the internet are insufficiently secure.”

Hacking cameras has become commonplace in modern warfare in recent years. Almost any camera installed on a city street, outside a home or business can be used to gather intelligence.

Ukrainian hackers hijacked Russian surveillance cameras to monitor Russian troop movements and direct long-range strikes.

The technique was used by Kyiv during the first use of an undersea drone strike against a Russian submarine docked in the port of Novorossiysk.

Israeli security officials warned that Iran had used private security cameras to find targets for drone and missile barrages against Israel.

Research released earlier this year found hundreds of devices had been accessed as part of the Islamic Republic’s long-range campaign after the first US-Israeli attacks in late February.

But most notably, Israeli spies and the CIA managed to force their way into a network of security and traffic cameras across Tehran, locating Ali Khamenei, the former supreme leader, before launching the air strikes that killed him on the first day of Iran war.

The practice is now considered easier and cheaper than using drones and satellites to gather intelligence.

It also aids operational surprise because most camera owners are blissfully unaware their devices have been penetrated by hackers.

Ground-based cameras offer a unique perspective on the terrain, which isn’t the case with conventional aerial-based spy kit.

title: Bryson DeChambeau should be massively encouraged by what’s happening in golf this week while he’s away from the cameras
description: Bryson DeChambeau has some big decisions to make at the end of this year. The two-time US Open winner will see his current LIV Golf contract expire after this season, and his future is far from certain.
fullText:
Bryson DeChambeau has some big decisions to make at the end of this year.

The two-time US Open winner will see his current LIV Golf contract expire after this season, and his future is far from certain.

LIV Golf has lost its Saudi funding, raising major questions about whether the tour will even exist in 2027 and beyond. DeChambeau was seen speaking to PGA Tour officials about his future at The Masters, and he’s floated the possibility that he’ll do content creation full-time and only play the majors next year.

DeChambeau is currently on a practice run for that idea. He will not play competitive golf in between the US Open and The Open Championship because of the cancellation of LIV Louisiana, so right now he’s out of the spotlight.

But what has happened in the world of golf with DeChambeau not playing is great news for his future.

YouTuber Brad Dalke’s performance on the DP World Tour this week is one of the shocks of the golfing season. He was given a sponsor’s exemption to play the BMW International Open, and he’s two shots off the lead through 36 holes.

Dalke is an exceptional golfer, having played at The Masters and the US Open in 2017, but he doesn’t keep a full tour schedule and is instead a full-time content creator on YouTube.

So the fact that Dalke can turn up for his professional debut on the DP World Tour and compete immediately gives DeChambeau a template. It is possible to perform at your best in competitive golf while creating content.

This isn’t a weak field on the DP World Tour. Joaquin Niemann, who was in the top 10 at the US Open, and Sergio Garcia are just two of the highly regarded names competing in Germany this week.

So Dalke’s efforts so far are some much-needed encouragement for DeChambeau ahead of The Open in two weeks’ time. Now, if he can compete at Birkdale, then he’s laid out the blueprint for 2027, and we might see him step away from full-time golf.
